description: We are Team Os Mitos! We are aerospace enthusiasts using AI and microgravity combustion data to improve fire safety. Our interests span Space Exploration, Earth Orbit, and Education. We need creative minds skilled in Coding, Software, Data Analysis, or Graphic Design. Join us to innovate!
summary: We developed a 4D Physics-Informed Forensic Digital Twin for the NASA ACME s-Flame mission aboard the ISS. To overcome the limitations of sparse telemetry and hardware anomalies in microgravity, our solution integrates hybrid CAD reverse-engineering, Ansys Fluent CFD optimization, and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Our model accurately reconstructs the full 3D spatial behavior of the spherical flame, predicting thermodynamic signatures and radiative flux. This digital twin successfully recovered blind sensor data (ACME-DEV-026) and isolated thermal anomalies, matching the exact stoichiometric flame radius of 7.71 mm predicted by the Cantera GRI-Mech 3.0 kinetic model. This project is important because it recovers critical scientific data that would otherwise be lost to sensor limitations, enabling the design of safer habitats for the Moon and Mars before a fire even starts.
details:
What it does and how it works: Our solution creates a continuous 3D thermodynamic field of the ACME s-Flame experiment from sparse, fixed-position telemetry, with the live interactive simulation available at https://sflame-twin.streamlit.app. It maps the exact geometric boundaries of the flight hardware, applies real thermal boundary conditions, and uses a 4D PINN (Physics-Informed Neural Network) coupled with Navier-Stokes and Darcy-Forchheimer models to calculate volumetric temperature gradients and radiative flux.

Benefits and intended impact: Microgravity combustion testing is expensive and often limited by hardware failures. Our digital twin recovers lost telemetry (such as the sub-100°C thermal wave missed by Type B thermocouples) and maps hidden thermal anomalies (like the +53.4% CH* asymmetry caused by a 1.8mm support tube). The intended impact is to provide a high-fidelity, low-cost platform to understand microgravity fires, ultimately ensuring safer space exploration habitats.

Tools and technologies used: We used Python, PyTorch (for PINNs), Autodesk Inventor (for procedural and manual aerospace CAD modeling), Ansys Fluent (for CFD mesh optimization and simulation), OpenCV (for multimodal computer vision and frame filtering), Cantera with GRI-Mech 3.0 (for chemical kinetics benchmarking), and Streamlit (for hosting the interactive 3D web platform at https://sflame-twin.streamlit.app).

How it is creative: We replaced complex physical 3D mesh supports in the "Far Rake" with Virtual Point Probes (X,Y,Z) in Ansys Fluent, eliminating mesh skewness and accelerating solver convergence. In our AI architecture, we implemented a differentiable radial compactification technique to solve the periodic aliasing of Fourier features in the far-field, ensuring absolute thermodynamic stability.

Factors considered: We rigorously audited NASA's official engineering documents to account for flight waivers and hardware deviations (e.g., ACME-DEV-031, ACME-DEV-046). We also accounted for the 650 ms exposure time of the ACME DataCam by implementing mathematical temporal compensation to accurately synchronize optical data with the 125 Hz telemetry.
